div1.head: Interview with Joseph L. Thomas, Sr. [8/29/2006]

sp.speaker: Barbara Purkey
sp.p: Today is Tuesday, August 29,2006. We are at the Dundalk Historical Society with Mr. Joseph L. Thomas. Mr. Thomas is 79 years old and was born August 22, 1927. He served in the Merchant Marines and the Army in WWII and my name is Barbara Purkey.

sp.speaker: Barbara Purkey
sp.p: Mr. Thomas do you want to start by telling us where you were born and raised?

sp.speaker: Joseph L. Thomas, Sr.
sp.p: I was born in Fort Howard, Md.

sp.speaker: Barbara Purkey
sp.p: Where did you go to school?

sp.speaker: Joseph L. Thomas, Sr.
sp.p: I went to the Fort Howard, School.

sp.speaker: Barbara Purkey
sp.p: They had the school right there.

sp.speaker: Joseph L. Thomas, Sr.
sp.p: They had a school there and it has been torn down to make way for the Veterans Park they are building there.

sp.speaker: Barbara Purkey
sp.p: What was your Mom's and Dad's name?

sp.speaker: Joseph L. Thomas, Sr.
sp.p: My Mother's name was Amelia and my Father's name was Eugene. They both came from France. They had 5 children here, 3 boys and 2 Daughters and all boys went into the Military. My Mother and Father were not American Citizens when we went into the service but the FBI kept questioning my Father about his American Citizenship Papers so my Father cold went through the classes and got his American Citizenship papers. That way, he did not have to worry about getting deported back overseas. My Mother, it took her five times to take the test and never did pass the test. When she passed away, she was still a French Citizen.

sp.speaker: Barbara Purkey
sp.p: Where did you go to High School?

sp.speaker: Joseph L. Thomas, Sr.
sp.p: Sparrows Point High.

sp.speaker: Barbara Purkey
sp.p: Did you graduate?

sp.speaker: Joseph L. Thomas, Sr.
sp.p: No, I didn't because at that time things were very hard and we had to work for support. Jobs were very hard and could not get enough money in the household so the boys had to get out and go to work.

sp.speaker: Barbara Purkey
sp.p: Where did you go to work?

sp.speaker: Joseph L. Thomas, Sr.
sp.p: Well, we worked mostly on Todd's Farm. We worked in the fields, stables, barns and helped clear fields to make way to grow stuff. Most of the time we took and worked on the farm and our day would start at 3 in the morning. Dad would wake us up and we would have to go to the Farm and I was just a little toddler but I could still rake the horse's stalls. We fed the horses, watered them and hooked them up to the wagon. Load the wagons with burlap sacks or baskets for whatever they were going to pick in the fields that day. We would distribute them along the edges of the fields. Then when that was done, we would come back, unhitch the horses, wipe them down, water them and then go home. On the way home, we would go through the swamps to check on muskrat traps as we used to sell their hides. We would clean and wipe the hides down and then go in the house and eat breakfast and get ready for school.

sp.speaker: Barbara Purkey
sp.p: Oh my goodness, you had a long day.

sp.speaker: Joseph L. Thomas, Sr.
sp.p: Yeah, then we would go to school which was less than a block from our house so we had no trouble getting to school. Then when school was over, come home and change clothes, re-check the muskrat traps and by that time is was getting near dark. We would return to the farm, check the horses and wipe them down, clean the stalls, hook the horses back up and go out to the fields and bring in the spinach or kale or whatever they picked that day and load up the wagons and take them back to the bam. We prepared the kale and spinach with ice and loaded them up on the truck and send them off to the market. By this time, it was dark and we did not have electricity but we did have well water so we headed home and we had to do our homework by oil lamp. We had outdoor spot a pots, if that is what you want to call them. We would do our homework and Mom would fix the supper and we would sit down. We had a flat buckeye stove that we used for heating and cooking. Mom would prepare her meals on it. I never ate a piece of store bought bread until I went in the service. We always baked our own bread at home.

sp.speaker: Barbara Purkey
sp.p: You were lucky.

sp.speaker: Joseph L. Thomas, Sr.
sp.p: Oh man, do I miss that! That is how we were raised down at Fort Howard. We were in the barracks at Fort Howard and I had an Uncle in the Military that was stationed there. General McArthur, he lived down there in Fort Howard.

sp.speaker: Barbara Purkey
sp.p: Is that right?

sp.speaker: Joseph L. Thomas, Sr.
sp.p: Oh, yeah. He lived down there in one of those houses. They had all Military and while my Uncle was there, we used to go down and watch them parade on the parade grounds. That was all inside the Fort but we lived outside Fort Howard. Then we moved just outside the gate one time moving a house from one side to the other side of the property. While we was doing that we moved into a house right outside the gates. We went to school in rain or snow because there were no days off for weather. The Army truck used to bring Military Kids out the Fort in the truck and a lot of times when nobody was looking, the soldiers used to pick us up and take us too because we had about a mile and a half to go to school. No snow plows in those days either.

sp.speaker: Barbara Purkey
sp.p: No, I don't think so. When did you join the Merchant Marines?

sp.speaker: Joseph L. Thomas, Sr.
sp.p: The war broke out and my brothers and cousins were going off to war and I was not old enough. I wanted to get in there and I was not old enough for the draft. My brothers and cousins got in there first and was going to war. I wanted to go and wanted to help out. So I had this baptisimal paper that I doctored up that made me 16 years old because a news article came out that anybody 16 years old could join the maritime service. My little forgery on my part, battle Mom and Dad first, and they finally agreed to let me go. I signed up and they shipped me by Silver Meter Train down to Florida, St. Petersburg, Florida where there was a Maritime Base there. That is where I took my maritime training down there.

sp.speaker: Barbara Purkey
sp.p: Will you talk a little bit about your training?

sp.speaker: Joseph L. Thomas, Sr.
sp.p: Well, we training first of all on a sailing ship and it was just like a Navy Base. They had all military training and you scrubbed your clothes on tables outside. Then we trained, the first ship was a sailing ship that had swinging hammocks on it. Then we went on to a coal burning freighter that they had there for training us all about the engine room and the engines. Then they brought in another ship one time that had turbo engines in it. It was the newest thing out and all of us in the advanced classes went aboard that thing and was instructed on how to run the engines on that thing.

sp.speaker: Barbara Purkey
sp.p: So you were in the engine room, mostly.

sp.speaker: Joseph L. Thomas, Sr.
sp.p: The engine room, yes, that is what the red stripe is for, then I graduated from there. Well first of all, we had to earn the life boat captain's license. They would take you out in the Gulf of Mexico and set you adrift in life boats. They would disappear and you would have to figure out which way to go, how to survive and you had to command the crew in the boat. I found my way back.

sp.speaker: Barbara Purkey
sp.p: Was it scary?

sp.speaker: Joseph L. Thomas, Sr.
sp.p: Well, yeah, it got a little rough. The Mississippi River comes out into the Gulf of Mexico and even on a calm day there is 7 foot waves.

sp.speaker: Barbara Purkey
sp.p: There you are in a life boat!

sp.speaker: Joseph L. Thomas, Sr.
sp.p: Yeah, you have to figure to put up with the current and go the opposite way of the current. You had to rig up a sail and compensate all of that. I ended back up near my destination.

sp.speaker: Barbara Purkey
sp.p: What did you do for food?

sp.speaker: Joseph L. Thomas, Sr.
sp.p: We had rations in the life boat for 3 days. If you survived or got back to your destination close to the time, we was 10 miles away compared to the 60 that we started with. They had planes watching us also, my boat was one of the first ones back in. They had no problems with the boats. Then we learned about gunnery, the 20 mm, we had to learn to shoot them. They were in the turret, the ship had about six turrets, you know. I call it boat but it was a ship. When we completed the course they loaded us up into a bus for Houston, Texas. We was on the bus rounding a mountain near New Orleans and it was raining and we came around the curve and somebody had dropped a big chunk of concrete and bricks on the road and the bus driver swerved to miss that and the bus went off the road and rolled over. They had to radio into New Orleans and sent an ambulance, the police and another bus. It was like 45 of us on the bus and I will say about 5 out of the 45 were hurt so they took them off into the ambulance and we went on the other bus and continued onto Houston, Texas. They assigned us to ships and I was there I guess about a week and a half. I liked it there because all the men were in the Military and the girls was piled up at the gate every night when we got off. I didn't spend a nickel in Texas because the girls treated us everywhere. They took us to their homes, to carnivals and we didn't have to report until 6 in the morning for roll call and then we had the rest of the day off and be back at 6 at night. On the weekend, they would only let you have one weekend off, I met two girls, one named Eva Earp, a relative of the Wyatt Earp Family. Edna Mae Lee was one of the heirs to the Robert E. Lee Family and they had a "36 Ford convertible and they took me everywhere. I think it was Eva Earps' Family, had a Dude Ranch and we would go out on the horses and shoot jack rabbits and we had a big barbecue with lights and music. We had a good weekend. After that I got called to go into Corpus Christi, boarded a ship there and delivered Aviation Gas across the Gulf of Mexico just about the time there was a hurricane working there. The Gulf of Mexico coming out making big waves and the hurricane making big waves the other way, we had one rough time in the Gulf of Mexico. We was towing a gasoline ship and we had some planes come out of Pensacola with colors, orange was the students and blue was the instructors, and we had radio silence so we used signal flags. Because of the rough surf, the signal flags got covered with soot and we had to take them down and when we went to pull them up again, but before we got them up, here comes these 4 planes out of Pensacola. They were trying to give us a little "straffing" job as to, "Hey, who are you?" We had to hurry up and get the flags back up.

sp.speaker: Barbara Purkey
sp.p: Oh, they didn't know if you were an enemy ship.

sp.speaker: Joseph L. Thomas, Sr.
sp.p: They didn't know. Anyway, we went on and we gave out our fuel and went back to Corpus Christi and took another tanker out. We had to go into the South Pacific but no destination. We went out and met Navy Ships and refueled them at sea. Then we came back to Corpus Christi because that was a big oil refinery back there. From there, I headed for home thinking I was away enough and my family wanted to see me. It was hard to keep in touch with family because I was on the move so much there was no place to mail letters.

sp.speaker: Barbara Purkey
sp.p: So you got leave?

sp.speaker: Joseph L. Thomas, Sr.
sp.p: Yeah. When you sign off a ship you got leave to go sign up on another ship.

sp.speaker: Barbara Purkey
sp.p: Oh, I see, you can do that when you want to.

sp.speaker: Joseph L. Thomas, Sr.
sp.p: Yeah. I came on home for a brief tour, a couple of days here at home and then I went to Fells Point to a Union Hall down there. I was not Union, I was just what you called Federal, I worked for no union, just a seaman. I finally caught another ship out of Baltimore here, I can't remember the name, and we started across the North Atlantic, very rough. In fact, I have never seen the North Atlantic calm. We was in convoy and after awhile we had to split up, go so far and then, re-rendezvous again. We split up but we must have been the Lone Ranger out there somehow and I was in the engine room working. The generator deck is about 20 feet above your head where they have the great big diesel generator and all of a sudden you hear a great big, "whomp" and the whole side caved in and a torpedo was sticking right through there! The whole side of the ship and water was just pouring in. The Chief Engineer said to pump all the liquid to the Port side of the ship so the ship would raise up because being up in the generator deck, it wasn't that far under water. It got it above water after we started pumping everything to give it a heavy lift, water fuel and everything. They had a repair ship in the area but I didn't know who it was operated by but it was sailors and they came over with a big crane, divers to go underwater and they took the cable and put it around the fins of the torpedo and they backed their ship way off and let the cable off so that if it did blow, they wouldn't get, just us. They pulled it out and they said what had happened, was that the torpedo hit the ship at an angle and the torpedo had firing pins sticking out of the front. By hitting on an angle, the firing pins were bent and it did not explode. That was a Liberty Ship.

sp.speaker: Barbara Purkey
sp.p: Wow, you got lucky on that one, huh?

sp.speaker: Joseph L. Thomas, Sr.
sp.p: Yeah, but I would rather have been on top side ..

sp.speaker: Barbara Purkey
sp.p: Yeah, I guess so.

sp.speaker: Joseph L. Thomas, Sr.
sp.p: Well, we got that torpedo out and they had divers come over and they welded a make shift plate over the hole and burnt some of metal out but it still leaked and we had to pump it out until we got to England.

sp.speaker: Barbara Purkey
sp.p: Oh, ok, you went ahead and went to England.

sp.speaker: Joseph L. Thomas, Sr.
sp.p: Yeah, then we pulled it into a shipyard into the dry dock, raised it up and unloaded the ship while it was in dry dock. They put all the cargo on to another ship and took the plate out and welded it or whatever they had to do so that it was not leaking anymore. Then we went back to the States.

sp.speaker: Barbara Purkey
sp.p: Did you go into town while you were in England?

sp.speaker: Joseph L. Thomas, Sr.
sp.p: No, we were not allowed to go into town. They had so many service men in town, Army, Navy and they could not afford to let anyone get lost, you know, if they had to ship out right away. Things were hot to trot.

sp.speaker: Barbara Purkey
sp.p: Well this was in the early' 40' s and England was being bombed at this point, right?

sp.speaker: Joseph L. Thomas, Sr.
sp.p: Right. Noise and run.

sp.speaker: Barbara Purkey
sp.p: Now while you were there were there any bombs there?

sp.speaker: Joseph L. Thomas, Sr.
sp.p: We could hear in the distance but nothing near us. Anyway we got into Norfolk and we caught another one going back and we went all the way back to England. We were in the English Channel off the White Cliffs of Dover and the tide is running. We had to put both anchors over and keep both propellers of the ship turning and the engine running in order to stand still in the current while we waited for some more ships to come up, we needed 4 or 5 ships because the LST boats, they were the guys that guided us past all the wreckage in the English Channel.

sp.speaker: Barbara Purkey
sp.p: What kind of wreckage.

sp.speaker: Joseph L. Thomas, Sr.
sp.p: All kind of ships and everything.

sp.speaker: Barbara Purkey
sp.p: You mean from gun battles.

sp.speaker: Joseph L. Thomas, Sr.
sp.p: Yeah, they had to guide us through the wreckage, you know. While we were laying at anchor with both chains out, the Germans would come down and lay mines down and when the tide would ebb, the LST's were out there, American and English, with mine sweepers cutting them loose and when they would pop up into the surface, they would blow them up with rifle fire.

sp.speaker: Barbara Purkey
sp.p: Oh, my goodness. It was all going on in the channel.

sp.speaker: Joseph L. Thomas, Sr.
sp.p: They missed one of them. It came right down between our anchor chains.

sp.speaker: Barbara Purkey
sp.p: Oh, you could see it?

sp.speaker: Joseph L. Thomas, Sr.
sp.p: I didn't see it, I was in the engine room. A couple of guys were sick so we had to work in the engine room then come up and take bow watch. I had just come out of the engine room because I was supposed to go up and take bow watch. Even when you are at anchor, you do bow watch. One of the ordinary seaman, can't remember his name. I came up from the engine room, all sweaty and got a cup of coffee and grabbed a coat to go up to the bow and he says, "Go ahead, dry off, get your coffee and I'll go up to the bow for you." That is when the mine hit and I never seen him anymore and I could not tell you his name, even. He was on the bow and that mine blew number one hole and most of number two hole off. The ship took off down the current and there was nothing we could do to control it.

sp.speaker: Barbara Purkey
sp.p: The ship was just floating on down.

sp.speaker: Joseph L. Thomas, Sr.
sp.p: With the current. An American LST and the British LST chased us and they was shooting these grappling hooks because we could not stop. By the time they caught us, we were way down by the Rock of Gibraltar. They got us in tow and had to hold still until the tide stopped running so they could tow us up the current and we went into a little port in France. They had like a dry dock, it raised up in the air with a slant and I don't know what they call that. They took the ship and it took 18 days to weld steel plates with eyebeams on the inside to make a point so we could cut water. They had to take all the cargo off. The food and clothing ended up in the bow and trucks and jeeps were in the hold in the back and they were saved. All the other stuff went. They put a make shift plate on the bow and mean time things were stirring up pretty bad. They said, " You are Americans, get that steel helmet and get on that truck." We loaded on the truck and 18 days we were up front.

sp.speaker: Barbara Purkey
sp.p: What do you mean by "up front?"

sp.speaker: Joseph L. Thomas, Sr.
sp.p: Where the shooting was going on.

sp.speaker: Barbara Purkey
sp.p: This was in France.

sp.speaker: Joseph L. Thomas, Sr.
sp.p: You know when they were having the battle of the bulge or something like that.

sp.speaker: Barbara Purkey
sp.p: You had not been trained with a gun or anything?

sp.speaker: Joseph L. Thomas, Sr.
sp.p: We were trained for the big guns but not rifles.

sp.speaker: Barbara Purkey
sp.p: So they give you a helmet and a rifle?

sp.speaker: Joseph L. Thomas, Sr.
sp.p: Yeah and I mashed the hell out of my thumb the first time just trying to load it. I had a mighty sore thumb.

sp.speaker: Barbara Purkey
sp.p: My goodness, here you are finding yourself heading up to the front lines and how old were you?

sp.speaker: Joseph L. Thomas, Sr.
sp.p: I was about 17. I wasn't even in the military but the Merchant Marines.

sp.speaker: Barbara Purkey
sp.p: You were an American and you needed to go.

sp.speaker: Joseph L. Thomas, Sr.
sp.p: Yep, an American waiting for a ship, get on that truck. We will be back and they did come back and got us. They found us but we were not all together. Two or three on one truck and two or three on another, you know, but they rounded us all up.

sp.speaker: Barbara Purkey
sp.p: How long were you out there?

sp.speaker: Joseph L. Thomas, Sr.
sp.p: 18 days. We came back and went back to the port where the ship was launched and we got on board, all our belonging were there except for what was stolen. We got back out to sea and they said to wait for an ebb tide because of the bow going against the current, our little problem. We were in dock for about 3 or 4 hours and got the engine running. It didn't hurt the engine or boilers or nothing. Just the holes up in the front of the ship. We brought her back to New York and went into the Brooklyn Shipyard. We signed off the ship and we had to go to the Brooklyn Shipyard.

sp.speaker: Barbara Purkey
sp.p: That was when you got to go home.

sp.speaker: Joseph L. Thomas, Sr.
sp.p: That was when I got my sea bag stolen. I had a friend of mine who had an apartment with his wife and he was the carpenter on the ship and he told me to stop on my way home. He said he had something for me so I stopped there on my way home. He lived at the top of the steps at an apartment and the cab pulled up, got my sea bag out of the trunk and we opened the door because it was raining so hard that the windows were rattling. I put my sea bag down and went up the top of the steps, knocked on the door and he opened it up. I told him I wouldn't come up because I had my sea bag sitting downstairs and we talked a bit, about 5 or 10 minutes and that was when my sea bag disappeared. How they opened those doors without all that noise that it made when I opened them, I'll never knOw. They were gone. I said to my friend that I heard a car but didn't know if it was just somebody going by. They notified me about finding a lot of stolen stuff a couple of years later and did I want to identify it. My sea bag had all the ships names stenciled on them, seaman's papers, discharges and the only thing I saved was money in my pocket and put my pea coat on because it was raining and it was chilly and that was all I went home with. A pea coat and a wallet with a couple of bucks in it. My Father got mad at me and didn't talk to me.

sp.speaker: Barbara Purkey
sp.p: Because you lost your stuff?

sp.speaker: Joseph L. Thomas, Sr.
sp.p: Oh yeah, "You lost your stuff, that is stupid." Well, it was just one of those things.

sp.speaker: Barbara Purkey
sp.p: Here you were coming off of a ship with all that experience and being hit by a sea mine.

sp.speaker: Joseph L. Thomas, Sr.
sp.p: A spike mine. You know, one of those balls with all the spikes. That is why it was easy to shoot because you could miss one and hit two or three others. It doesn't take much to make them go off

sp.speaker: Barbara Purkey
sp.p: So did you get some time to recover from all of that?

sp.speaker: Joseph L. Thomas, Sr.
sp.p: Well, like I said, when I got back I had 30 days leave coming to me. On my way home, one of the reasons my Dad got mad at me, I didn't go right home, I went to the draft board over here. I wanted to go into the Army. I was tired of the Sea.

sp.speaker: Barbara Purkey
sp.p: So, he really didn't want you joining the Army.

sp.speaker: Joseph L. Thomas, Sr.
sp.p: No. He said I was dumb for losing my stuff and dumb for signing up. So I said what was I going to do I am of draft age. He said I could have taken my leave time anyway.

sp.speaker: Barbara Purkey
sp.p: He probably missed you.

sp.speaker: Joseph L. Thomas, Sr.
sp.p: Out of the three sons, the oldest was in the Army and his tank got a hit while on maneuvers and killed 2 guys in the tank and like shell shocked him so he wasn't worth much or could not do anything in the house. He was of no help to Dad and the other was too young, so, here I was, just ready! Somebody had cut the wood, chop the kindling, run the traps, somebody had to do it. You have to gut them, skin them out, dry them and salt them down. Then you pack them and sell them. He was just real mad when I signed up for the Army but everybody was in the service. I wanted to be in the Army.

sp.speaker: Barbara Purkey
sp.p: Even after you were out there with a gun, that did not discourage you?

sp.speaker: Joseph L. Thomas, Sr.
sp.p: Nope. To this day, I would go again. I guess it is in your blood because my son was the same way. My son was spit and polish, an academy man, couldn't get a bit of dirt under his fingernails, all Military. He went into the service and like I say, he was going to make a life career and put 21 years in but a year and a half was Vietnam and they really dosed him with agent orange and today he is 100 percent disabled living in Columbus, Georgia. The Government is looking after him going to the hospital 2 or 3 times a week. They got him a nice van with hydraulic this and everything for his wheel chair. They are treating him good but he is suffering, has no life. He cannot walk except with a walker when he can walk. I feel sorry for him because all his young life went down the drain. He has a family, four kids. Two of them twins and two boys and 2 girls. They are very well educated and have traveled with him all over the world. They were in Germany while he was on 3 tours there, North Pole and they could not understand why they had to go to bed when it was still day light.

sp.speaker: Barbara Purkey
sp.p: Well, getting back to when you were going in the Army, did you have to go through Boot Camp?

sp.speaker: Joseph L. Thomas, Sr.
sp.p: Oh, yeah. They had me in Camp Meade and from there I went by train to Fort Leonard Wood, Missouri. That is where I took my Boot Training.

sp.speaker: Barbara Purkey
sp.p: Do you remember anything about your training?

sp.speaker: Joseph L. Thomas, Sr.
sp.p: Oh, yeah, it was in the Ozark Mountains, lots of snow, very cold, hard on your fingers on the rifle range. In them days, they had rat races and they have outlawed them since then. We would go in the barracks and if somebody made a noise after lights are supposed to be out the Sgt. would come in and yell, "Ok, I give you three minutes and you will be outside with a rain coat on, with a combat boot on one foot and a rain boot on the other foot and your rifle over your head." The rifle weighs about 9 pound and you hold it over your head and run around the barracks 10 times. You get around the barracks half way and that rifle gets heavier and heavier and if he catches it down on your head, you run another five times around. That was what they called, rat race. That was just one of the maneuvers. Since then they outlawed it because some of the boys passed out.

sp.speaker: Barbara Purkey
sp.p: Sure, I guess it was too physical.

sp.speaker: Joseph L. Thomas, Sr.
sp.p: It was too much physical. Then I went into training of automatic mechanizing. I was mechanic for diesels and when I was in Boot Camp being that I had previous experience in the Military, I was always the Platoon Leader. I was the one that yelled, "Hup, two, three, four." On the weekends when everyone got a weekend off, the Captain would say, "You go up in the quarters and answer the phone." I had very few weekends off because I always got stuck up there. The only thing good was he had a bottle in the bottom drawer! It was so cold in the Ozark Mountains and when you go out on a 10 mile hike it is a 10 mile hike but in the snow, it is like 110 miles. It is hard to walk in the snow and some of it was 2 feet deep with no trails that had been walked. It was very rugged training, they put you through the ropes and you have to give it to them, it was all for your benefit. Of course, you froze half the time but they knew when to stop. When we completed Boot Camp Training, some went off to cooks and bakers and some went to mechanized mobile and others went to other stuff. I was in the mechanized mobile.

sp.speaker: Barbara Purkey
sp.p: Was that tanks?

sp.speaker: Joseph L. Thomas, Sr.
sp.p: That is anything mechanized with anything from a scooter to a Sherman Tank. Then you had to learn to drive all these things besides fix them. You had a license for each one and I had 54 driver's license. I drove anything from a legal cargo cart with a 4 cylinder motor in it and you load anything on it and all the way up to a Sherman Tank. You had to know how to operate them and if it breaks down in combat in the field, you have to know how to drive it. That was pretty good and was interesting. I know it was very interesting and was something I would use the rest of my life.

sp.speaker: Barbara Purkey
sp.p: Sure, you learned how to fix a lot of different motors.

sp.speaker: Joseph L. Thomas, Sr.
sp.p: The Maritime Service, all those ships aren't easy. Today, I am still a big boater. I have my own boat and my buddy has one and we go fishing and crabbing. We work on our own. Anyway, too rough with the cold weather and the rat races but we all survived it. Some got sick but it all went pretty good. Then graduation ceremonies, President Truman, Oh, second Lt. Emerald Truman, a nephew of the President. I befriended him and he got me out of a couple of jams, like, late for guard duty or late for this and that. On graduation day we were dressed up in the field and the President came over with his nephew and shook my hand and he said I was one of his good friends.

sp.speaker: Barbara Purkey
sp.p: Wow, that is a memory to remember.

sp.speaker: Joseph L. Thomas, Sr.
sp.p: A bunch of guys all jumped on me after that.

sp.speaker: Barbara Purkey
sp.p: Why is that? Because you were somebody special.

sp.speaker: Joseph L. Thomas, Sr.
sp.p: Anyway, we shipped out of there to New Jersey.

sp.speaker: Barbara Purkey
sp.p: New Jersey was for what?

sp.speaker: Joseph L. Thomas, Sr.
sp.p: That is the station where they ship you out to different places. My organization was the 32nd Engineer Battalion, that is where it broke up .. We had the training that we had and we were some needed here and some needed there and that is where the Battalion split up. We got shipped out and eventually we all come home.

sp.speaker: Barbara Purkey
sp.p: Where were you shipped out to?

sp.speaker: Joseph L. Thomas, Sr.
sp.p: Over, Camp Top Hat, Germany. They were still very cautious about letting you go out of Camp so you could not go out sight seeing.

sp.speaker: Barbara Purkey
sp.p: Tell me about food. Did they have a kitchen set up and all of that?

sp.speaker: Joseph L. Thomas, Sr.
sp.p: Yeah, I'll say it wasn't bad but when you are a Merchant Seaman, you eat like a King on the ship. In the Army, well, you know.

sp.speaker: Barbara Purkey
sp.p: A big come down.

sp.speaker: Joseph L. Thomas, Sr.
sp.p: A big let down! But, we were alright. There were days when you had to eat rations because there was nowhere you could cook anything. They had a kitchen at Camp Top Hat with your breakfast at 6 but sometime you had to wait until 8 to get it. There were so many in and out. Sometime we missed lunch because we were too occupied to eat. You ate so much at one meal and I never ate more than two meals a day anyhow. You ate a big breakfast and a big supper. I did the same thing in the Maritime. Lunchtime you just sit with the people and shoot the bull, you know. After a couple of weeks there they sent us back to the docks and loaded us on the ships. They sent us back.

sp.speaker: Barbara Purkey
sp.p: Sent you back to the States?

sp.speaker: Joseph L. Thomas, Sr.
sp.p: Yeah. Nobody ever said why and they sent us home and they gave us a week leave. During that week I got pretty upset and had to go to the hospital at Fort Meade and they kept me there for awhile. Then, they eventually discharged me. They called it war nerves.

sp.speaker: Barbara Purkey
sp.p: Now something had happened at Camp Top Hat.

sp.speaker: Joseph L. Thomas, Sr.
sp.p: No, no. Nothing happened, nothing that I knew of. We went to work there repairing and getting things back to shape and all that stuff All of a sudden, we came back to the barracks and they said, "Pack it up, we are going out!" No, why, you don't question them.

sp.speaker: Barbara Purkey
sp.p: Well, lucky for you.

sp.speaker: Joseph L. Thomas, Sr.
sp.p: Yeah, the only thing I didn't like, when I was over there a couple of times, the buildings that were blown down, there were a lot of people under the rubble. Talk about a stench, my God, you cannot believe the smell. You could put handkerchiefs over your mouth but it did not help one bit because the stench was so bad. When they went through the town, they just blowed everything up. Very, very strong odor that made you sick. Talking about being sick, when I did go overboard when that mine hit the ship and the English picked me up.

sp.speaker: Barbara Purkey
sp.p: I did not know you went overboard!

sp.speaker: Joseph L. Thomas, Sr.
sp.p: Yeah, some of us went overboard.

sp.speaker: Barbara Purkey
sp.p: Gee, you didn't tell me that!

sp.speaker: Joseph L. Thomas, Sr.
sp.p: That water is rough and cold and when they dragged me out of that water and put me on this English Ship, they fed me this cotton picking tea but it was "Yuk" for me and to this day, I will not drink tea!

sp.speaker: Barbara Purkey
sp.p: That bad. How long were you in the water?

sp.speaker: Joseph L. Thomas, Sr.
sp.p: About 2 hours.

sp.speaker: Barbara Purkey
sp.p: Did you have life jacket?

sp.speaker: Joseph L. Thomas, Sr.
sp.p: Oh yeah, life preservers and life line that was hanging off the ship but it took two hours to get us down.

sp.speaker: Barbara Purkey
sp.p: That was when the ship hit the mine?

sp.speaker: Joseph L. Thomas, Sr.
sp.p: When the mine hit the ship.

sp.speaker: Barbara Purkey
sp.p: Well, I thought you were down below.

sp.speaker: Joseph L. Thomas, Sr.
sp.p: I was down below but had come up to drink a cup of coffee. The little seaman told me to go and drink my coffee and cool off

sp.speaker: Barbara Purkey
sp.p: Oh, the bow got hit and if you had been there, you would have been hit.

sp.speaker: Joseph L. Thomas, Sr.
sp.p: I started out the door with my coffee and put my coat on because I was all sweaty. He said cool off with my coffee and he would sit there until I was done. He relieved me because he was off

sp.speaker: Barbara Purkey
sp.p: You wound up in the water and I can imagine that was cold.

sp.speaker: Joseph L. Thomas, Sr.
sp.p: Darn right it was cold.

sp.speaker: Barbara Purkey
sp.p: Yeah, for two hours a person could get hyperthermia.

sp.speaker: Joseph L. Thomas, Sr.
sp.p: The current was so much that your energy from your body keeps you warm, I guess. By the time they chased us down and pulled us in.

sp.speaker: Barbara Purkey
sp.p: This was when the ship was being pulled away and you are hanging on a rope and being pulled. That was pretty rough!

sp.speaker: Joseph L. Thomas, Sr.
sp.p: Well, you are going with the flow. It is not like you are standing and the flow is going by you, you are actually going with the flow. It was rough and could see the other ships chasing us to get around and shoot the hooks, so we knew they were trying to grab us. They did and when they got to us and put the brakes on, that is when they hurried up and got us out of the water. The tide was starting to ease off a little bit.

sp.speaker: Barbara Purkey
sp.p: You have had a lot of excitement for a young man but you are back home, getting a discharge and heading back to the farm.

sp.speaker: Joseph L. Thomas, Sr.
sp.p: No. I live over here in West Inverness now.

sp.speaker: Barbara Purkey
sp.p: You mean when you came back out of the Army, you didn't go back to the farm?

sp.speaker: Joseph L. Thomas, Sr.
sp.p: Oh, when I came from the Army, that was just a brief temporary thing back to the Army. I only worked a small time at the farm and then I met another girl, I had gotten married when I was in the Army. Soon as I left, so did she. I came back on an unexpected leave one time and caught her in the apartment with some other guy. I got a divorce. After I got discharged out of the Army, I met this other girl and went with her, got married, have five children and have a home here in West Inverness. I have been there for 51 years.

sp.speaker: Barbara Purkey
sp.p: How long were you in the Army all together?

sp.speaker: Joseph L. Thomas, Sr.
sp.p: I was in the Army not too long. About one year and three years in the Merchant Marine.

sp.speaker: Barbara Purkey
sp.p: About 4 years all together. That was long enough.

sp.speaker: Joseph L. Thomas, Sr.
sp.p: I had excitement.

sp.speaker: Barbara Purkey
sp.p: What was the name of your wife? You said you married her.

sp.speaker: Joseph L. Thomas, Sr.
sp.p: Number one wife was Marie, number two wife was Jeanette and number three wife was Mary.

sp.speaker: Barbara Purkey
sp.p: And she had children.

sp.speaker: Joseph L. Thomas, Sr.
sp.p: No. 1 wife, she did not have children. I have been married three times. In the Army I had the first wife, after being discharged, second wife Jeanette and we had 5 children. She died in'76 and in , 83 I married this woman here and her name is Mary. Now, every time of think about it, I make the sign of the cross for Mary and Joe.

sp.speaker: Barbara Purkey
sp.p: You also have two grandchildren.

sp.speaker: Joseph L. Thomas, Sr.
sp.p: Oh, my God, we have. This woman here had 6 children and I had 5 and they had kids and their kids had kids. The last time we counted, it was somewhere around 30 or 32 grandchildren and somewhere 7 or 8 great grandchildren. I told them have all the fun they want and keep on going.

sp.speaker: Barbara Purkey
sp.p: Where did you go to work?

sp.speaker: Joseph L. Thomas, Sr.
sp.p: I worked 33 years at Bethlehem Steel and retired from Bethlehem Steel.

sp.speaker: Barbara Purkey
sp.p: As a mechanic?

sp.speaker: Joseph L. Thomas, Sr.
sp.p: Well, I was a mechanic for the first 20 and the last I was a welder.

sp.speaker: Barbara Purkey
sp.p: What have you done since you retired? You have a boat.

sp.speaker: Joseph L. Thomas, Sr.
sp.p: I have a boat and I do a lot of crabbing and fishing. My daughter owned a trucking company and before I retired, I was working for her driving a tractor and trailer. Then I still have trouble with me knee and back and since I was a welder, I just stayed in the shop at the Marine Terminal and did welding on the trucks instead of driving them. A couple of years ago I retired from there.

sp.speaker: Barbara Purkey
sp.p: Two retirements.

sp.speaker: Joseph L. Thomas, Sr.
sp.p: Two. Right now I get Social Security, Pension from Bethlehem Steel and taking care of a sick wife.

sp.speaker: Barbara Purkey
sp.p: We are just about finished now and I think we have covered everything. Do you have any thoughts on the war that you would like to share with us.

sp.speaker: Joseph L. Thomas, Sr.
sp.p: Yeah, I do. I think this Iraq War was very thoughtless, very thoughtless. I think, my own opinion, his Father went in there and cut them off short. He only run them out of one place and this Bush gets in there and feels that he will finish what Dad started. It is very stupid move, he should never have to go back in there and they have found nothing.

sp.speaker: Barbara Purkey
sp.p: I think a lot of Veterans think this is a different kind of war.

sp.speaker: Joseph L. Thomas, Sr.
sp.p: It is definitely a different kind of war. You don't even know who the enemy isl It could be a 10 year old kid or whatever! For no reason at all, he just went in there and made a fool of us. He is down grading the American Name for doing a stupid thing like thatl

sp.speaker: Barbara Purkey
sp.p: Well, we want to thank you for coming in and talking to us. We appreciate it.

sp.speaker: Joseph L. Thomas, Sr.
sp.p: I do appreciate your having me in here.

sp.speaker: Barbara Purkey
sp.p: Thank you.
